caption: The Milky Way over the Next Generation Transit Survey, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way arches over the Atacama Desert in this view from ESO's Paranal Observatory. In the foreground sits a planet-hunting facility called NGTS, the Next Generation Transit Survey, while ESO telescopes stand in the background.

NGTS was built by a team of UK, Swiss and German institutions and is made up of 12 telescopes. Together they watch the sky without pause, tracking the brightness of hundreds of thousands of stars. When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view, the star dims very slightly, and NGTS is designed to catch that small drop.

Its speciality is super-Earths, planets heavier than our own but lighter than an ice giant such as Neptune. Behind it, the Very Large Telescope shines its adaptive optics lasers into the sky, and the survey telescope VISTA stands to the right. These larger telescopes help check what NGTS finds.
explore: Once NGTS spots a promising planet candidate, ESO instruments take over. HARPS at La Silla Observatory and ESPRESSO at the Very Large Telescope can follow up, and such observations reveal how massive these planets are and what their atmospheres are made of.

caption: Twilight panorama of the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: This wide panorama shows ESO's Very Large Telescope on Cerro Paranal at twilight. The low Sun lights up frost on the ground and lends the whole observatory a soft glow, while stars already fill the sky above. On the right stand the boxy, angular Unit Telescopes, and on the left are the curved, open domes of the smaller Auxiliary Telescopes.

The VLT is really eight telescopes, and seven of them are visible. Four are large Unit Telescopes with 8.2-metre mirrors, and four are movable 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes, three of which are in view. Because the small ones can be moved, the VLT can work as an interferometer, combining light from several telescopes so that they act together like one much larger instrument.

The remote site has real advantages. It offers some of the driest and clearest skies on Earth and no light pollution, and the image was captured under tough conditions by ESO photo ambassador Miguel Claro.
explore: Getting there takes effort. There is no public transport, so visitors drive from Antofagasta airport in the north or make a 110-kilometre trip north from the closest town. Free public tours run every weekend and can include a Unit Telescope, the La Residencia hotel and sometimes the control rooms.

caption: Laser guide stars from the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Beams of laser light shoot from ESO's Very Large Telescope into the Chilean night sky. It may look like science fiction, but the lasers are there to create artificial stars that help the telescope see more sharply.

The problem they solve is Earth's atmosphere. Turbulent air makes stars appear to twinkle and blurs the images that telescopes record. Placing observatories high in a dry desert helps, because there is less air to disturb the light, but modern telescopes go further with a technique called adaptive optics.

The lasers make sodium atoms glow about 90 km above the ground, producing guide stars to use as reference points. A computer watches how the atmosphere distorts them and bends a flexible mirror to cancel the distortion, adjusting it up to 1000 times per second. The result is a much clearer view of whatever the telescope is studying.
explore: ESO's Extremely Large Telescope, which is being built, will use the same laser system. It will also house the biggest telescope mirror ever made, so astronomers expect even sharper images of the Universe.

caption: The Milky Way above the Residencia, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The plane of the Milky Way stretches across the sky above the Residencia, the hotel where astronomers stay at ESO's Paranal Observatory. Staff members walking past have stopped to take in the view.

The Residencia, designed by the German architects Auer+Weber+Assoziierte, is a refuge in one of the harshest landscapes imaginable. The Atacama Desert brings extreme dryness, intense ultraviolet light from the Sun and high altitude as part of daily life for those working at the observatory.

Those same conditions make the nights exceptional. The Residencia and the Very Large Telescope sit far from sources of light pollution and enjoy very clear air. On moonless nights the sky can be so dark that the Milky Way's light is enough to cast a shadow on the ground. That makes the site valuable for high-quality science and, as this photograph shows, for astrophotography too.
explore: Luis Calçada, who works as a motion graphic designer at ESO's headquarters in Garching, Germany, took this photograph.

caption: Orion rising over the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The constellation of Orion, the Hunter, with his well-known belt and sword, rises over the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope (SEST) at ESO's La Silla Observatory. Just above the three stars of the belt, the Orion Nebula shows its blue and pink hues.

Orion lies on the celestial equator, so it can be seen from both hemispheres. The Orion Nebula within it is a stellar nursery where hundreds of new stars are forming. Telescopes have found many young stars there wrapped in cocoons of gas and dust, which are expected to become protoplanetary discs, the flattened material from which planets can grow, as the stars mature.

To the left of the dish, the reddish giant stars Betelgeuse, in Orion, and Aldebaran, in Taurus, trace a curved line towards the ground. Near the horizon the line meets a fuzzy group of stars, the Pleiades cluster.
explore: In classical mythology, Orion was a hunter who pursued the Pleiades, the daughters of Atlas, in search of love. The pairing on the sky here, with the Hunter above and the cluster low near the horizon, echoes that old story.

caption: A reddened twilight sky over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: An unusually red twilight glows above the dark silhouette of Cerro Paranal, where ESO's Very Large Telescope points up at the sky beneath the Milky Way. The colour was caused by a volcanic eruption thousands of kilometres away.

On 15 January 2022 the southern Pacific Ocean saw the undersea volcano Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha‘apai erupt. Its shock waves spread through the atmosphere, and weather stations at ESO's Paranal and La Silla observatories, more than 10 000 kilometres away, recorded the disturbance.

The eruption also threw an ash plume 57 kilometres high, loading the atmosphere with particles such as water vapour and dust. Tiny dust particles scatter sunlight and make it redder, an effect several ESO telescopes picked up in their twilight calibration images. This photo was taken 6 months after the eruption, showing that the effect lasted well beyond the event itself.
explore: By the time ESO published the picture, a year after the eruption, the sky had still not returned to the state it was in before the volcano erupted, a sign of how long such fine particles can linger high above the ground.

caption: ALMA antennas under the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: Moonlit and patient, four ALMA antennas, part of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, point up at a star-filled sky. Moonlight illuminates the scene from the right, and the band of the Milky Way runs across the upper left.

When this picture was taken, ALMA was still being built at 5000 m altitude on the Chajnantor plateau in Chile's Atacama Desert. The site is one of the driest on Earth, and that dryness, together with the thin air at high altitude, makes it ideal for observing at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, forms of light with wavelengths far longer than the eye can detect.

At those wavelengths astronomers can study molecular clouds, dense regions of gas and dust where stars form when a cloud collapses under its own gravity. The Universe was still relatively unexplored in submillimetre light, so astronomers expected ALMA to reveal new secrets about how stars, galaxies and planets begin.
explore: Europe, North America and East Asia run ALMA as partners, working with the Republic of Chile. It combines the efforts of many countries to build and run the array. ESO Photo Ambassador José Francisco Salgado took the photograph.

caption: The Southern Cross over the Danish 1.54-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The Danish 1.54-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory looks out at the southern sky with its dome open. To the left of the dome, set in the plane of the Milky Way, is the Southern Cross, one of the most distinctive star patterns in the sky.

The Cross is formed by Alpha, Beta, Gamma and Delta Crucis, four stars of the constellation Crux. They are not neighbours in space. The nearest, Gamma Crucis, is just 88 light-years from Earth, while the most distant is 364 light-years away. Alpha Crucis, a blue-white star at the bottom of the Cross, ranks as the 13th brightest star anywhere in the night sky.
Just above the Cross lies a dark smudge, the Coalsack Nebula. It is a cloud of interstellar dust that blocks the light of stars behind it, leaving what looks like an empty patch in the Milky Way.
explore: Below the Cross are two patches of glowing gas, the red emission nebula IC 2948 and the Carina Nebula. The photo comes from the Ultra High Definition Expedition to La Silla.

caption: A Unit Telescope of the Very Large Telescope under the night sky, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Lit only by the night sky, one of the Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope stands out in this picture. Across the top right, the Milky Way traces a colourful path, with the dust lanes and star-forming regions of our galaxy clearly visible.

Few astronomical facilities in the world match the VLT in size and sophistication. Its four Unit Telescopes are identical, and each main mirror measures 8.2 metres across. Each is a large telescope by itself, but light from all of them can also be combined in an arrangement called an interferometer. At its longest baseline, this can resolve details 25 times finer than a single telescope can manage.
The observatory sits 2635 metres above sea level in the Atacama Desert. The air there holds so little water vapour that the VLT can observe infrared light as well as visible light.
explore: The display of stars is itself a demonstration of the site's excellent observing conditions, since the dark, dry sky lets the camera record the dust lanes and star-forming regions of the Milky Way in detail.

caption: Two ALMA antennas beneath Orion, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: Two antennas of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) stand together on the Chajnantor Plateau on a winter night. Above them hangs the constellation of Orion, the Hunter, recognisable by his starry belt, with the red supergiant Betelgeuse marking his shoulder on the right of the photo.

These are two of the 66 antennas that make up ALMA, in which ESO is a partner. They observe in millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, which are hard to catch from the ground because water vapour in the atmosphere absorbs them. Telescopes working in this light must sit very high, where the air is drier. ALMA's antennas therefore stand at 5000 metres.
Betelgeuse lies just under 650 light-years from us. It is a prime target for ALMA's kind of observations, as is the nearby Orion Nebula.
explore: The plateau can feel very isolated on winter nights, but it offers some of the driest and darkest skies anywhere, which is exactly what ALMA needs to work well.

caption: The Milky Way and Barnard's Loop over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The central plane of our galaxy curves gently across this photograph from ESO's La Silla Observatory, dotted with bright patches of gas and threaded with dark, winding lanes of dust. At first it is a little hard to pick out against the busy background, but the constellation of Orion, the Hunter, sits at the top left.

Several pink clouds appear to spread beyond the band of the Milky Way. Their faint glow comes from ionised hydrogen gas, a sign that hot, young stars are nearby. One of them is Barnard's Loop, which wraps around the famous Orion Nebula and can be traced curving around Orion's Belt.
Beneath this colourful sky sits the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope. It has been used to chase the aftermath of gamma-ray bursts, which are among the most energetic explosions in the Universe.
explore: The same telescope carries the Wide Field Imager (WFI), a camera it uses to take pictures of the nearby cosmos. The photograph was taken by ESO Photo Ambassador Yuri Beletsky, who captured the sky above La Silla in rich detail.

caption: ALMA antennas under the Moon and Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: This panoramic view of the Chajnantor Plateau shows ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, with several antennas working together under a clear, star-filled sky. The ground seems to curve, but that is an effect of the wide-angle lens. The Moon crowns the top of the image, and the Milky Way shows as a hazy stripe, partly washed out by moonlight.
Dark patches inside the Milky Way's band are places where interstellar dust blocks the light of stars behind it.

The plateau lies at 5000 metres in the Chilean Andes and ranks among the finest sites on Earth for astronomy. ALMA is described as the world's most powerful telescope for studying the Universe at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths. When this picture was published, it was in an early science phase, not yet fully built, yet already outperforming all other submillimetre arrays. Construction was expected to finish in 2013 with a total of 66 antennas.
explore: The photo was taken by ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi, founder and leader of The World At Night, a project that photographs landmarks against the night sky. ALMA is run by partners in Europe, North America and East Asia with Chile. ESO, NRAO and NAOJ lead for each region, and the Joint ALMA Observatory manages it.

caption: A meteor over the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: A meteor streaks across the starry, dust-streaked Milky Way above ESO's La Silla Observatory. Watching from the left side is a silent, retired telescope, the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, or SEST.

ESO and the Swedish Natural Science Research Council had SEST built in 1987, and it was retired 16 years later. Throughout that time it looked up at some of the darkest, clearest skies anywhere. When it was built, the 15-metre dish was the southern hemisphere's only large telescope designed for submillimetre astronomy, which studies light with wavelengths longer than infrared.
Over its working life SEST took on many kinds of research, including observations of the centre of the Milky Way and of our galaxy's two satellite galaxies, the Magellanic Clouds.
explore: In 1995, SEST observations showed that the Boomerang Nebula, a gas cloud cast off by a dying star in Centaurus, was the coldest known place in the Universe. Its temperature was measured at only one degree above absolute zero.

caption: The Milky Way over the Danish 1.54-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way, with its bright central region, stretches over the Danish 1.54-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory, lighting up the Chilean desert sky. The telescope has been at work since 1979, uncovering details about our home galaxy.

It was used for a survey lasting 15 years, published in 2004, that studied 14,000 stars in our galaxy. The project measured the stars' motions and distances, along with their ages and chemical make-up. From these, astronomers built a historical map of the Milky Way.

That map showed a far more complicated past than anyone had expected. The galaxy looks calm in this photo, but the survey found traces of a turbulent and violent history. In particular, collisions with smaller galaxies brought in huge gas clouds that set off bursts of star formation and supernova explosions, events that helped shape the galaxy we live in today.
explore: The survey gave the first clues to this restless history. By combining where stars are, how they move, how old they are and what they are made of, astronomers could read the Milky Way's past much as geologists read layers of rock.

caption: A shooting star over the ExTrA telescopes, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: A shooting star flashes across the night sky towards the horizon of the Atacama Desert, above two of the three new ExTrA telescopes at ESO's La Silla Observatory. The telescopes sit more than 2000 meters above sea level and search for Earth-sized planets around M class stars, which are smaller than the Sun.
Despite the name, a shooting star is not a star at all. It is a small piece of rock or dust that burns up as it enters Earth's atmosphere. Before that happens, such a fragment is called a meteoroid.
These streaks are useful as well as pretty. By following the path and brightness of a meteoroid, scientists can trace its origin within the Solar System and learn its composition.
explore: If a meteoroid survives its fall through the atmosphere and reaches the ground, it becomes a meteorite. Meteorites are studied closely for what they reveal about the Solar System's past.

caption: Laser beams from Unit Telescope 4 of the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Powerful laser beams leave Unit Telescope 4 of ESO's Very Large Telescope in the Atacama Desert. They are aimed at a layer of the upper atmosphere about 90 kilometres up, which is rich in sodium atoms.

The lasers' colour is tuned to excite those atoms so that they shine like stars. Astronomers use these artificial stars to measure how Earth's turbulent atmosphere blurs light arriving from space. That information drives a deformable mirror, which corrects the blur in real time. The technique is called adaptive optics, and it gives much sharper observations.

This telescope, also called Yepun, is the only VLT telescope fitted with a Laser Guide Star Facility. Every beam is 30 centimetres wide and carries 22 watts of power. For safety, cameras watch the patch of sky the lasers pass through, and the lasers are switched off quickly if an aircraft is seen approaching.
explore: Unit Telescope 4 also goes by the name Yepun. The guide stars it creates are not real stars at all but patches of glowing sodium high in the atmosphere, and the deformable mirror that relies on them keeps changing its shape to undo the blurring as it happens.

caption: The Great Rift above the VISTA telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Dark lanes cut across the brightest part of the Milky Way above ESO's VISTA telescope at Paranal Observatory, so that the glowing region seems to play hide-and-seek with the telescope. These dark lines are known as the Great Rift.

The Rift is made of vast clouds of gas and dust lying between the Solar System and the inner Milky Way. They soak up most of the visible light from the billions of stars at the centre of our galaxy. Astronomers can still study the inner Milky Way, though, because infrared and radio light pass through the clouds without being absorbed, letting telescopes effectively look through the Rift.

VISTA, the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy, stands on the peak next to the one holding the Very Large Telescope. It is one of the largest infrared survey telescopes, helping to map the Universe and study questions such as how galaxies evolve.
explore: Infrared telescopes such as VISTA are well suited to peering past dust. Where the eye and ordinary cameras see only darkness in the Rift, infrared light reveals the stars that lie hidden beyond.

caption: Venus over the BlackGEM telescopes, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Venus shines brightly over ESO's La Silla Observatory in this photo taken just before dawn, looking east. The sky also shows the soft zodiacal light, which is sunlight bounced off tiny grains of dust spread through the Solar System. To the left of the road stand the three domes of the BlackGEM telescopes.

Radboud University, KU Leuven and the Netherlands Research School for Astronomy (NOVA) built BlackGEM. Its task is to hunt for the fading glow left by some of the Universe's most violent events, such as collisions of black holes and neutron stars.

Such crashes send ripples through space and time that the LIGO and Virgo observatories can detect. Thanks to their wide field of view, the BlackGEM telescopes can spot the visible glow left behind by these events and so pinpoint where each collision took place.
explore: Knowing where a merger happened lets astronomers study in greater detail what goes on when black holes and neutron stars merge, adding visible light to the ripples in spacetime that first announced the event.

caption: Comet Lemmon and a laser test at the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A laser beam shoots from ESO's Very Large Telescope into a sky full of stars, with the Milky Way arching overhead. It may look like a futuristic laser cannon aimed at some distant invader, but it was captured during tests of a new laser for the VLT.

The laser was destined to play a key role in the VLT's Laser Guide Star Facility. This system lets astronomers correct most of the disturbance caused by the constantly moving atmosphere, producing much sharper images.

There is a second treat hidden in the picture. Right of centre, just below the Small Magellanic Cloud and almost lost among countless stars, sits a small green dot trailing a faint tail to the left. This is Comet Lemmon, then newly discovered and brighter than expected, which was moving slowly through the southern skies.
explore: The photograph was taken by ESO Photo Ambassador Gerhard Hüdepohl on 14 February 2013, while engineers were testing the laser at Paranal. The same frame also caught Comet Lemmon moving through the southern sky.

caption: The ESO 3.6-metre telescope under the Large Magellanic Cloud, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The ESO 3.6-metre telescope sits on the summit of La Silla, 2400 m above sea level in the Atacama Desert. At the top of the picture shines the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy that orbits our own Milky Way.

The site offers ideal conditions for watching the sky. The desert air is dry and clouds are rare, and being far from cities keeps the sky dark. A faint green airglow near the horizon comes naturally from molecules high in Earth's atmosphere. Even the warm, dim lights along the access road at the bottom of the frame are meant to keep light pollution low.
This telescope is home to HARPS, the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher, a highly productive planet-hunting instrument.
explore: In the Mapuche culture, the Large Magellanic Cloud goes by lafken, labken or künchalabken, meaning lagoon, and by rünanko, meaning water well. It is one of the Milky Way's neighbouring galaxies.

caption: Orion over the ESO 3.6-metre telescope walkway, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: The constellation of Orion, the Hunter, looks down on a small walkway at ESO's La Silla Observatory. The walkway links the ESO 3.6-metre telescope with the Coudé Auxiliary Telescope, which is no longer in use.

This long exposure by ESO Photo Ambassador Yuri Beletsky hides several details. On the right, a streak of light marks an artificial satellite passing behind the telescope dome. A faint reddish arc curves around the bright Orion Nebula. This is Barnard's Loop, an emission nebula thought to be what remains of a supernova, the explosion of a star. Just below the walkway and running alongside it, the dark dust lanes of the Milky Way ripple across the stars.
The 3.6-metre telescope carries HARPS, the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher, counted among the most accurate and productive planet-hunting instruments astronomy has ever had.
explore: HARPS, as its full name suggests, hunts for planets by measuring radial velocity, the tiny shifts in a star's motion towards and away from us caused by the pull of orbiting planets.

story: A pink haze fills the bottom of this frame, while the blues and whites of the Milky Way spread above. The blocky shapes in the foreground are the Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory, and a harsh yellow slash cuts right through the scene.

That streak is the VLT's laser guide star. It belongs to the telescope's adaptive optics system, which works to undo the blurring caused by the atmosphere. As light from space passes through the air, small local differences in the atmosphere distort it.

To correct for this, astronomers usually look for a bright star close to their target and use it as a reference. When no suitable star lies near enough, they make their own, shining a bright laser into the night sky to create an artificial one.

caption: Comet 252P/LINEAR above the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A soft green glow sits just above the Milky Way in this sweeping panorama, between the galaxy's starry arch and a Unit Telescope of ESO's Very Large Telescope at the centre of the frame. That glow is Comet 252P/LINEAR, photographed in April 2016.

In late March 2016 this comet came closer to Earth than almost any comet on record, at just over 5.3 million kilometres. Halley's Comet, by comparison, came no closer than 87 million kilometres. Instead of a classic long tail, 252P/LINEAR shows a round glow tinted green by molecules of diatomic carbon fluorescing in sunlight.

The dark skies above Paranal offer much more. The Milky Way's clouds are crowded with stars, colourful natural airglow lines the horizon, and high overhead two planets join the red supergiant Antares in a slightly lopsided triangle, with bright Mars to the left and whitish Saturn below.
explore: Paranal sits in the vast Atacama Desert under the dark southern sky, which makes it an excellent place to spot comets. ESO counts it among the most spectacular observatory sites on the planet.

caption: Airglow and the Milky Way over the Swedish–ESO Submillimetre Telescope, La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: ESO's La Silla Observatory sits beneath a shimmering sky in this image. Deep reddish tones fill the right side and fade into the Milky Way, and a red and greenish-yellow glow colours the scene. In the foreground, taking centre stage, is a silver dish, the Swedish–ESO Submillimetre Telescope, or SEST.

The colourful glow is airglow, light produced by Earth's own atmosphere. It is normally seen only from space or from very dark places, and La Silla has some of the darkest, clearest night skies on Earth.

SEST was retired in 2003 and no longer observes, but it remains a favourite subject for photographers, reflecting the lights and colours of the sky. Behind it is the rounded dome of the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, home to the planet-hunting instrument HARPS.
explore: HARPS, the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher, is described as the world's leading exoplanet hunter, having found more low-mass exoplanets than any other planet-hunting instrument so far. The photo is by ESO Photo Ambassador Yuri Beletsky, an astronomer at ESO who takes such images in his spare time.

caption: The Auxiliary Telescopes under the Magellanic Clouds, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The four Auxiliary Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope stand against a sky thick with stars on Cerro Paranal. Hanging above the site are the Small and Large Magellanic Clouds, two objects that can only be seen from the southern sky.

Each Auxiliary Telescope has a mirror 1.8 metres across. Together with the four larger Unit Telescopes, whose mirrors are 8.2 metres across, they make up what ESO calls the world's most advanced optical observatory.

The telescopes can combine their light to form the VLT Interferometer, or VLTI. Working this way, they let astronomers see details up to 25 times finer than a single Unit Telescope can show. The Magellanic Clouds overhead are irregular dwarf galaxies in the Local Group, our galaxy's neighbourhood, and they are companions of the Milky Way.
explore: The picture was taken by John Colosimo, who shared it through the Your ESO Pictures group on Flickr, where members of the public post their own photographs of ESO sites and skies.

caption: Construction of the Extremely Large Telescope under the night sky, Cerro Armazones, Chile
story: This view of the construction site of ESO's Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) comes from one of the webcams that watch over it. Taken on 3 May 2025, it shows how far building work has come, with the frameworks of both giant dome doors, which will open at night, now in place.

On the far right, a bright orange glow rises into the sky. These are lasers, and although they seem aimed at the meteor to the left, they have a gentler job. They belong to the adaptive optics system of ESO's Very Large Telescope, making artificial guide stars that help correct for atmospheric turbulence and sharpen astronomers' images.
The lasers make sodium atoms glow in a layer of the upper atmosphere about 90 km above the ground. Those atoms were deposited there by meteors, much like the one in the frame.
explore: When it is finished, the ELT will also use laser guide stars, six of them, to help it deliver very sharp images of the cosmos. The webcams let ESO follow the telescope's progress day and night.

story: One of the Auxiliary Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope seems to point straight at a green, emerald-like glow high above it. That glow is Comet 252P/LINEAR.

The comet was discovered in April 2000 and has only fairly recently arrived in the inner Solar System, travelling between the orbits of Jupiter and Earth. In March 2016 it passed especially close to our planet, at only 5.2 million kilometres, which ranks it as the fifth closest comet passage ever recorded. At the time this picture was released, it could still be seen from the southern hemisphere.

Its green colour comes from carbon-based gas around the comet that fluoresces, glowing as it absorbs sunlight. Comets are icy bodies, and as they near the Sun they release gas and dust that can form a glowing cloud around them, as this one does.
explore: The picture was taken by ESO Photo Ambassador Babak A. Tafreshi at the start of ESO's Fulldome Expedition, a project to capture more pictures from ESO's observatories and of the southern night sky.

caption: The heart of the Milky Way above three Unit Telescopes, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The crowded heart of the Milky Way, packed with gas, dust, star clusters and glowing nebulae, forms the backdrop for three of the Very Large Telescope's Unit Telescopes lined up in a row. From left to right they are Antu (UT1), Kueyen (UT2) and Melipal (UT3). In the Mapuche language these names mean the Sun, the Moon and the Southern Cross.

The VLT, run by ESO on Cerro Paranal in northern Chile, has four Unit Telescopes with 8.2-metre main mirrors, the fourth being Yepun. They usually work separately, and one of them can record objects as faint as magnitude 30 in an hour-long exposure, about four billion times fainter than the unaided eye can see.
Joined together with four movable 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes, they form the VLT Interferometer, which can see details up to 25 times finer than a single telescope.
explore: Inside the VLTI, beams of light meet through a system of mirrors in underground tunnels, where the path lengths over a hundred metres must match to within a tiny fraction of a millimetre. That precision lets it make images sharp enough, in principle, to tell apart a car's two headlights at the distance of the Moon.

caption: The VLT Auxiliary Telescopes under a starry sky, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Flecks of blue, orange and red fill the sky above ESO's Paranal Observatory. Each one is a star, a galaxy, a nebula or something else, and together they make up the sparkling view that astronomers study as they try to understand the Universe.

On the ground stand three of the four movable VLT Auxiliary Telescopes. These smaller telescopes feed light into the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, which ESO describes as the world's most advanced optical instrument.

Working together, the telescopes can do far more than any one of them alone. By combining their light, they act like a single, much larger telescope, and can reveal details that would otherwise only be visible to a telescope as wide as the distance separating them. The units are movable, and together they feed their light into the interferometer.

caption: Four VLT lasers and a diagram of the Unit Telescope layout, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Four laser beams stretch across the southern sky, one from each Unit Telescope of ESO's Very Large Telescope. At the time, the telescopes were working together as the VLT Interferometer. Where a thin layer of cloud drifted through the beams, each one lit up with a glowing bead of light.

Those four bright spots form a pattern that mirrors the layout of the four Unit Telescopes that fire the lasers. This version of the image adds an overlay showing that layout, so the match between the spots and the telescopes on the ground can be compared directly.

The spots were a happy accident. The lasers are normally aimed at a far higher layer of the atmosphere, 90 kilometres above Earth's surface, where they make artificial guide stars used to correct for the blurring of the air. The cloud simply caught the beams on their way up, lighting them where they crossed it.
explore: Each Unit Telescope sends its own beam, so the pattern of glowing spots in the cloud acts almost like a map of the platform below, flipped as if seen in a mirror.

That shimmer is airglow. It comes from chemical reactions high in the atmosphere that give off light. Usually these emissions are fairly weak, but on the night this photo was taken they were much brighter than normal.

Each Auxiliary Telescope has a mirror 1.8 metres across. They are designed to work alongside one another as if they were a single telescope, combining their light through the VLT Interferometer. caption: The Milky Way arching over ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: The Milky Way curves across the Chilean desert sky, framing the ALMA antennas, part of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. Beneath its arc, two smudges mark the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, satellite galaxies of our own. On the ground, an artificial green light illuminates the antennas, contrasting with the natural display overhead.
ALMA sits more than 5000 metres above sea level. At that height the air is dry and thin, which gives an excellent view of the Universe and makes the site ideal for a sensitive instrument like ALMA.

ALMA is not one single telescope. It is made of 66 separate antennas spread over the Chajnantor plateau, and they can be moved. By arranging them in different configurations, astronomers can adjust how finely ALMA resolves the objects it observes.
explore: ALMA's antennas collect millimetre and submillimetre light, which is much longer in wavelength than the visible light captured in this photograph. The Magellanic Clouds, the faint patches below the arc, orbit the Milky Way as its smaller companions.

story: The four Auxiliary Telescopes at ESO's Paranal Observatory point up at a night sky packed with things to see. Its dark, pristine skies make Paranal a leading spot on Earth for studying the Universe,.

To the right of the band of the Milky Way are two cloudy patches that look like bursts of galactic fireworks. They are the two Magellanic Clouds, Large and Small, dwarf galaxies held captive by the Milky Way's gravity.

In the Mapuche language of south-central Chile, the Magellanic Clouds are called lafken, labken or künchalabken, meaning the lagoons, as well as rünanko, meaning the water wells. Juan Carlos Muñoz Mateos took the photograph, which shows how crowded the sky over Paranal can look on a dark night.

caption: The Laser Guide Star Facility under the southern sky, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Stars fill this night sky over Paranal Observatory, but other objects stand out too. At the bottom left is the pinkish Carina Nebula. Higher up shines a bright bluish star, Canopus, the second-brightest star in the night sky. To the right of Canopus lie the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, two bluish patches that are irregular galaxies neighbouring the Milky Way.

To study such objects in more detail, ground-based telescopes must overcome the turbulence of Earth's atmosphere, which blurs astronomical images. The Very Large Telescope tackles this with adaptive optics, helped by lasers fired from the Laser Guide Star Facility on Unit Telescope 4.

The lasers excite sodium atoms high in the atmosphere, which then give off light. That light is disturbed by moving air in the same way as starlight. By collecting it, the adaptive optics system can measure the atmosphere's distortions and correct for them.

caption: The Milky Way over the Atacama Desert near Cerro Armazones, Chile
story: The Milky Way stretches across this night landscape in the Atacama Desert, a region that has hosted ESO's observatories since the 1960s and that was chosen as the site of the Extremely Large Telescope. Our galaxy is a disc, and here we see it exactly edge-on.

Looking towards its centre, the galaxy's plane is crowded with a hundred thousand million stars, along with a great deal of gas and dust between them. The dust absorbs visible light and forms the prominent dark lanes crossing the bright band.

Follow one of those lanes, which seems to rise from the centre of the Galaxy towards the top, and you reach a yellowish nebula around the star Antares, also called Alpha Scorpii. Next to it is a bluish nebula around Rho Ophiuchi. The centre of the Galaxy is found in the direction of Sagittarius.
explore: The Extremely Large Telescope is described by ESO as the world's biggest eye on the sky. The photograph was taken by Gerhard Hüdepohl, looking towards the crowded central regions of our galaxy.

caption: The Milky Way over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The dark outline of the Very Large Telescope on top of Paranal Mountain stands out against a sky thick with stars. The sky here is so good that stars remain clearly visible right down to the horizon, above the clouds that usually cover the Pacific Ocean, only 12 km from the observatory.

The brightest area, crossed by strong dark lanes, is the central bulge of our galaxy, which we see edge-on. Rising through the galaxy's centre is a brighter vertical column, the zodiacal light. It traces the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun, the same plane in which the planets, the Sun, the Moon and the zodiacal constellations lie.
At the end of a dark lane that seems to hang down from the Galactic Centre shines the bright star Antares, also known as Alpha Scorpii.
explore: Zodiacal light is sunlight scattered by fine dust spread through the inner Solar System, which is why it follows the same path across the sky as the Sun and planets.

caption: Comet McNaught over the Atacama Desert, near Antofagasta, Chile
story: Comet C/2006 P1, better known as Comet McNaught, is seen here from the coast of Chile's II Region, near Antofagasta. The comet reached perihelion, its closest point to the Sun, in January 2007, and unexpectedly became the brightest comet in the previous 40 years.

Conditions for professional astronomy in this corner of the Atacama Desert are excellent, and the II Region is home to several major facilities. ESO's Very Large Telescope stands some 120 km south of Antofagasta and is described as the world's most advanced optical-infrared observatory on the ground.

When the photo was released, ALMA, the world's largest radio observatory, was being built at 5000 metres near San Pedro de Atacama. Cerro Armazones, a mountain 3046 metres high and about 20 km from Paranal, had been chosen for the Extremely Large Telescope.
explore: ESO Photo Ambassador Gerhard Hüdepohl took the photograph. Comets like McNaught are icy bodies that grow bright as they approach the Sun and release gas and dust, and this one surprised observers by how brilliant it became.

caption: A laser guide star aimed at the heart of the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A laser beam leaves the Very Large Telescope's 8.2-metre Yepun telescope and points straight at the heart of the Milky Way, the centre of our galaxy. Prominent dark lanes run across the Milky Way's plane. They are vast clouds of interstellar dust that block visible light.

The laser is part of the VLT's adaptive optics system. It makes an artificial star 90 km up, in the layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere. That star is a reference for correcting images and spectra for the blurring caused by the air.

The dust lanes hide the galactic centre from ordinary view, but Yepun's infrared instruments allow astronomers to look through them. With them they study the complex, turbulent core of the Milky Way, where a supermassive black hole lurks.
explore: The Very Large Telescope has four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes, of which Yepun is the fourth, known as UT4. They are joined by four movable Auxiliary Telescopes, each 1.8 metres across. The photograph was taken by Gerhard Hüdepohl, looking towards the crowded central regions of our galaxy.

The laser guide star is part of the VLT's adaptive optics system. It acts as a reference that lets the telescope correct its images for the blurring caused by the atmosphere, so astronomers can see finer detail than the turbulent air would otherwise allow.

caption: La Silla Observatory under the Milky Way, Chile
story: The bright band of the Milky Way stretches overhead in this view of La Silla, ESO's original observatory. Several of the many telescopes on the site are visible below, 2400 metres up in Chile's Atacama Desert.

The site enjoys around 300 clear nights per year and excellent viewing conditions, and the clear view of our galaxy here shows why. Over time it became the largest astronomical observatory of its kind.

Many of its telescopes were pioneers, paving the way for new kinds of astronomical technology that later shaped whole new generations of telescopes. The Very Large Telescope had a forerunner in the New Technology Telescope (NTT), while the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope (SEST) prepared the ground for APEX and ALMA, observatories that study the sky at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths.
explore: La Silla marked the 50th anniversary of its inauguration in 2019, the year this image was released. Its scientific output still ranks it among the most productive observatories in the world, half a century after it opened.

caption: Star trails over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Colourful curved lines of light trace the paths of setting stars above the telescope domes of La Silla, on the southern edge of the Atacama Desert. The stars were not really moving like this. A long exposure on a moonlit night recorded each one as a trail as Earth turned. The view also takes in an inversion layer in the atmosphere.

Near the horizon the trails are noticeably distorted in this telephoto view. It is a mirage, like the familiar distortion of the Moon or Sun when they sit low in the sky. Light rays are refracted and bent as they pass through the atmosphere, producing warped or even multiple images of an object.
ESO's La Silla site has telescopes that observe in optical and infrared light. Its largest optical telescope has a mirror 3.6 metres across.
explore: La Silla's high altitude of 2400 metres, its dark sky and its clear air, which reduces the atmosphere's distortion of incoming light, make it an ideal place for astronomy. The photograph was taken by Babak Tafreshi.

Each Auxiliary Telescope is 1.8 metres across. They observe at the same time, using interferometry to see as sharply as a single telescope as wide as the greatest distance between them, in this case 48 metres. The larger 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes are usually used on their own, so the four Auxiliary Telescopes were added to make full use of the interferometry laboratory.
The constellations in view are Ophiuchus (the snake-holder), Sagittarius (the archer), Scorpius (the scorpion) and Triangulum Australe (the southern triangle).

caption: The night sky over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: This photograph shows the night sky above ESO's La Silla Observatory. La Silla stands 2400 metres high in the southern Atacama Desert, with Santiago de Chile lying 600 km to the south, and it was ESO's original observing site.

ESO runs two major telescopes there, the ESO 3.6-metre telescope and the 3.58-metre New Technology Telescope (NTT). Their state-of-the-art instruments are built either entirely by ESO or by outside groups of institutions with substantial help from ESO.

La Silla also regularly hosts visiting instruments. These are attached to a telescope for a single observing run and then removed, so that the site's telescopes can take on different equipment from one observing run to the next. The observatory is also home to many national telescopes, such as the Danish 1.54-metre telescope and Switzerland's 1.2-metre Leonhard Euler Telescope.

story: An Auxiliary Telescope, one of four serving ESO's Very Large Telescope, looks up at the sky above Paranal Observatory. Overhead, the Milky Way shows as a bright band across the southern sky.

The Auxiliary Telescopes send their light into the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, or VLTI. Combining light from several telescopes increases the amount of data collected and sharpens the images the system can produce.

Paranal sits 2600 metres up in Chile's Atacama Desert and enjoys about 300 clear nights a year. The excellent observing conditions at Paranal, together with the VLT's advanced technology, let astronomers study the Universe in detail. Each Auxiliary Telescope is 1.8 metres across, and they send their light into the VLT Interferometer, or VLTI, which combines light from several telescopes to sharpen the resolution even more and produce crisper images of astronomical objects.

The Auxiliary Telescopes are not fixed in place. They can be moved along tracks to many positions on the VLT platform. That flexibility lets astronomers adjust the VLTI to fit what each observing project requires, rather than working with a single fixed arrangement of telescopes every night.

The Auxiliary Telescopes are 1.8 metres across and are used only for interferometry. By combining their light, this technique lets astronomers see details up to 25 times finer than a single telescope could show. Their arrangement can be changed by moving them between 30 different observing positions on the platform.
The Magellanic Clouds are nearby irregular dwarf galaxies. From the southern hemisphere they are easy to see with the unaided eye.

story: One ALMA antenna looks small beneath the Milky Way, which winds across the sky above the Atacama Desert in northern Chile. It is one of 66 dishes forming the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array.

The array is designed to observe the Universe at wavelengths between infrared light and radio waves, a range the eye cannot see. Light at these wavelengths carries information about some of the coldest regions of the Universe, the places where new stars are only just forming. It also helps astronomers learn about the earliest galaxies.

ALMA's dishes are spread across the high Atacama plateau. In this photograph, though, just one of them is set against our own galaxy, dwarfed by the sweep of the Milky Way snaking across the dark sky above it.

story: The Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope stand beneath a clear night sky at Paranal Observatory. Each one carries its own set of instruments.

Every instrument is custom-made for one way of studying the Universe and aimed at a different scientific question. The VLT's instrument programme as a whole is described as the most ambitious ever planned for a single observatory, covering all the main observing modes needed for most of today's leading research.

This well-equipped facility has opened a new age of discovery. Among its achievements are some notable astronomical firsts, including the first image of a planet outside our Solar System and the tracking of stars as they swing near the supermassive black hole in our galaxy's core.

story: Unit Telescope 4 of ESO's Very Large Telescope, named Yepun, shines a laser into the Milky Way, which stretches overhead as a bright band. The laser creates an artificial guide star.

That guide star belongs to the adaptive optics system on Yepun. By measuring how the atmosphere disturbs the artificial star's light, the system can correct for the same effects in astronomical images, making them clearer.

To the right stand the other three Unit Telescopes, named Antu, Kueyen and Melipal from left to right. Every one has a main mirror 8.2 metres across, placing them among the largest single-mirror telescopes anywhere. A single VLT telescope can detect objects four billion times fainter than anything visible to the unaided eye.

caption: The edge-on galaxy NGC 4762, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A bright streak slices across this Hubble image. It is the galaxy NGC 4762, seen edge-on, and scattered in the background are a number of other, far more distant galaxies.

Found in the constellation of Virgo, NGC 4762 lies about 58 million light-years from us. It belongs to the Virgo Cluster, which sits at the centre of the larger Virgo supercluster, the same supercluster that contains our own Local Group of galaxies.

Astronomers once thought NGC 4762 was a barred spiral. It has since been identified as a lenticular galaxy, a type that sits between an elliptical and a spiral. Seeing it edge-on makes its true shape hard to judge, but astronomers have identified four main parts to it, which are a bulge at the centre, a bar, a thick disc and a ring on the outside. Its disc is lopsided and warped, perhaps because it once swallowed a smaller galaxy whose remains settled into the disc and rearranged its gas and stars.
explore: The galaxy is also listed as VCC 2095 in the Virgo Cluster Catalogue, which covers just over 2000 galaxies. It hosts a LINER-type active galactic nucleus, a very energetic central region identified by particular spectral lines that act like atomic fingerprints, revealing what the region is made of.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 2217, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A brilliant bar of light shines at the heart of NGC 2217, a barred spiral galaxy found in Canis Major, the Greater Dog. Many stars crowd into its central region to form that luminous bar, and a set of tightly wound spiral arms surrounds it.
The galaxy lies roughly 65 million light-years from Earth and, at 100 thousand light-years across, is about the same size as our Milky Way.

Bars like this one are important to how such galaxies change over time. They help channel gas from the disc towards the galaxy's centre. There, the gas and dust either form new stars or feed the supermassive black hole at the core. These black holes, which range from a few hundred to more than a billion times the mass of the Sun, are found in almost all large galaxies.
explore: NGC 2217 is also known as AM 0619-271. The colour in this Hubble image was added using a ground-based survey, the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System, better known as Pan-STARRS.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 6744, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble's view of the spiral galaxy NGC 6744 shows a bright central region packed with old yellow stars. Farther out, dusty spiral arms appear in shades of pink and blue. The blue patches are full of young star clusters, while the pink ones mark regions where stars are actively forming, a sign that the galaxy is still very lively.

At first glance NGC 6744 looks like our own Milky Way, only bigger. It measures more than 200 000 light-years across, compared with about 100 000 light-years for our galaxy. The resemblance goes beyond size, because like the Milky Way it has a prominent core crowded with old stars.

More evidence of activity came in 2005, when a supernova named SN 2005at was discovered in the galaxy, though it does not appear in this image. It was a Type Ic supernova, which forms when a massive star collapses in on itself and loses its envelope of hydrogen.
explore: NGC 6744 lies about 35 million light-years away, in the southern constellation of Pavo. The picture combines observations in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light, including a filter that picks out the glow of hydrogen gas.

caption: The spiral galaxy UGC 9391, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the spiral galaxy UGC 9391, which lies about 130 million light-years away in the constellation of Draco. The galaxy played a part in measuring how fast the Universe is expanding today.

Inside UGC 9391 are Cepheid variable stars. These stars brighten and fade in a regular rhythm, and the length of that rhythm is linked to how bright they really are. By comparing that true brightness with how bright they appear, astronomers can work out their distance.

The galaxy also hosted a Type Ia supernova, a kind of stellar explosion whose brightness can likewise be used to judge distance, though it is not visible here. A team of astronomers used both the Cepheids and the supernova in this galaxy as part of their calculation of the expansion rate of the modern Universe, making it one step on a longer ladder of distance measurements.

caption: The galaxy cluster Abell 1413, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the galaxy cluster Abell 1413, over 2 billion light-years from Earth between the constellations of Leo and Coma Berenices. The scene is dominated by a large, strongly elliptical galaxy called MCG+04-28-097, whose halo of stars stretches for more than 6.5 million light-years.

Abell 1413 is called rich because it holds a huge number of galaxies, more than 300, bound together by the cluster's powerful gravity. Interactions among them heat the material in the cluster to almost 100 million degrees, so the cluster gives off strong X-rays.

The cluster also shows faint arcs. These come from gravitational lensing, in which the cluster's intense gravity bends space-time around it, distorting the light of galaxies that lie farther behind it into strange, stretched shapes.
explore: Abell 1413 is part of the Abell catalogue of over 4000 rich galaxy clusters, all relatively close in astronomical terms, whose light has travelled for less than 3 billion years to get here. Galaxies near the cluster's centre are very elongated, while those farther out are rounder. A version of this image was entered by Nick Rose into the Hubble's Hidden Treasures processing competition.

caption: The merging galaxy pair NGC 3921, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Tails, loops and a disturbed shape mark NGC 3921, a pair of disc galaxies late in the process of merging. The structure in this Hubble image is typical of what is left behind after such a collision.

Mergers play a large part in how galaxies evolve and are especially important in forming elliptical galaxies. Only a few merging systems are near enough to study in depth, however, and NGC 3921, in the constellation of Ursa Major, is one of them.

Observations suggest the two galaxies were roughly equal in mass and that they collided about 700 million years ago. The impact set off a burst of star formation. Earlier Hubble observations found over 1000 bright, young star clusters springing to life at the heart of the pair.
explore: NGC 3921 lies about 270 million light-years away. Judy Schmidt is acknowledged in the image credit alongside ESA/Hubble and NASA. The image comes from Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2.

story: This Hubble image shows NGC 5474, a dwarf galaxy in Ursa Major, some 21 million light-years from us. The word dwarf can mislead, since the galaxy holds several billion stars. It only seems small next to the Milky Way, which has hundreds of billions.

NGC 5474 belongs to the Messier 101 Group. The brightest member is the Pinwheel Galaxy, Messier 101, a well-known spiral whose clear, well-defined arms class it as a grand design galaxy, like Messier 81 and Messier 74.

Messier 101 has other neighbours in the group, and gravitational interactions with them may have helped give it its distinctive shape. In the same way, interactions with Messier 101 may explain the distortions seen in NGC 5474. Our own Local Group and the Messier 101 Group both lie within the Virgo Supercluster, which makes NGC 5474 a neighbour of ours in galactic terms.

story: This Hubble image shows NGC 3274, a relatively faint spiral galaxy in Leo, more than 20 million light-years from Earth. In the upper right is another galaxy, PGC 213714, which lies much farther from Earth.

The picture was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, which can see from ultraviolet light through to the near infrared. That range lets astronomers study many kinds of targets, from star formation nearby to galaxies in the most remote parts of the cosmos. For this image, observations through five different filters were combined, bringing ultraviolet, visible and infrared light together in one view.

Like all Hubble data, the image benefits from the telescope's position above Earth's atmosphere, which would otherwise blur the view. From orbit, the camera can return sharp, detailed images again and again.
explore: NGC 3274 was discovered in 1783 by Wilhelm Herschel. Much later, Hubble's cameras can study it in light that Herschel could never have seen, including ultraviolet and near-infrared wavelengths, and with far sharper detail.

caption: The interacting galaxies IC 2163 and NGC 2207, imaged by ALMA and the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two galaxies overlap in this composite image, and the one on the left, IC 2163, has taken on a shape like a human eye. Its companion on the right is NGC 2207. The picture blends Hubble Space Telescope images with observations from ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array.

The pair lies approximately 114 million light-years away, towards the constellation of Canis Major. The two brushed together, their spiral arms touching only at the outer edges, with IC 2163 passing behind NGC 2207. That glancing blow sent a tsunami of stars and gas rushing inwards through IC 2163's disc. The wave slowed sharply and piled up partway through the disc, creating bright ribbons of intense star formation and squeezed ridges of gas and dust that look like a pair of eyelids.
Glancing collisions of this kind are fairly common, but eye-shaped structures are rarely seen.
explore: Their rarity is probably because they do not last long. Such ocular shapes tend to survive only several tens of millions of years, a blink in a galaxy's lifetime. ALMA is a partnership of ESO, the U.S. National Science Foundation and Japan's National Institutes of Natural Sciences, in cooperation with the Republic of Chile.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1097 and its companion, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: The spiral galaxy NGC 1097 seems to wrap its arms around a much smaller companion, the elliptical galaxy NGC 1097A, visible at the top left. The pair lies about 50 million light-years away in the constellation of Fornax, and there are signs that the two have interacted recently.

NGC 1097 is a Seyfert galaxy, which means a supermassive black hole sits at its centre. Its core is fairly faint, though, suggesting that the black hole is not currently consuming large amounts of gas and stars. The most prominent feature at the centre is instead a ring of bright knots around the nucleus. Astronomers think these are huge bubbles of hydrogen gas glowing because ultraviolet light from young stars has ionised them, and they show that the ring is forming stars vigorously.
Bluish clusters of hot, young stars also dot the spiral arms.
explore: NGC 1097 has four faint jets, too faint to show here, that form an X from its centre and are the longest visible-light jets known for any galaxy. They are thought to be the remains of a dwarf galaxy that NGC 1097 tore apart and swallowed, possibly as long as a few billion years ago. The knots in the ring are thought to be about 750–2500 light-years across.

caption: The spiral galaxy UGC 9391, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The star-studded arms of the spiral galaxy UGC 9391 stand alone against a backdrop of far more distant galaxies, which appear only as faint swirls and smudges. Some much brighter stars in the foreground, far closer to home, are ringed with diffraction spikes, an effect of light interacting with Hubble's internal optics.

Found in Draco, close to the north celestial pole, UGC 9391 is 130 million light-years from Earth. It was imaged as part of a set of Hubble observations used to build the cosmic distance ladder, a chain of linked measurements that lets astronomers judge the distances to the most remote objects.

Distances can only be measured directly for fairly nearby objects, closer than about 3000 light-years. Beyond that, astronomers depend on relationships calibrated with closer objects. UGC 9391 let them compare two such methods, supernova explosions and Cepheid variable stars, in the same galaxy.
explore: Making distance measurements more precise helps astronomers pin down how quickly the Universe is expanding, one of Hubble's main science goals. This image was taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and combines visible and infrared light.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy IC 5201, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the barred spiral galaxy IC 5201 in the southern constellation of Grus, the Crane. Like about two thirds of the spiral galaxies in the Universe, our Milky Way included, it has a bar of stars cutting through its centre.

The galaxy was first spotted in 1900 by Joseph Lunt, a British–South African astronomer looking through a telescope at Cape Town Observatory. More than a century later, astronomers are still interested in it.

To make this image, Hubble used its Advanced Camera for Surveys, which can pick out individual stars in other galaxies. That ability makes it a powerful tool for tracing how different populations of stars were born, evolved and died across the cosmos. IC 5201 itself lies more than 40 million light-years away from us.
explore: A galactic bar is a long, straight concentration of stars across a spiral galaxy's centre, from which the spiral arms often seem to unwind. Bars are common enough that they are a normal feature of spiral galaxies rather than an oddity.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 2835, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The twisting pattern of NGC 2835's many spiral arms creates the illusion of an eye. Fittingly, this barred spiral lies near the head of Hydra, the water snake, a southern constellation. It is just over half as wide as the Milky Way.

Bright blue areas in its outer spiral arms show where near-ultraviolet light is being given off more strongly, a sign of recent or ongoing star formation. A supermassive black hole, millions of times the mass of the Sun, is known to sit at the galaxy's centre, though it cannot be seen here.

Hubble imaged NGC 2835 for PHANGS-HST, a large survey that studies the links between cold gas and young stars in many nearby galaxies. In this galaxy, cold, dense gas gives rise to large numbers of young stars in big star-forming regions.
explore: The survey expects to capture more than 100 000 star-forming regions and gas clouds in other galaxies, and aims to clarify how cold gas, star formation and a galaxy's overall shape are connected. It is part of the wider PHANGS programme, working with ALMA and the MUSE instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope.

caption: The irregular dwarf galaxy UGC 4879, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A scattered drizzle of stars across this Hubble image makes up the galaxy UGC 4879. It is an irregular dwarf galaxy, a type that is smaller and messier than most, without the sweeping swirl of a spiral or the tidy shape of an elliptical.

UGC 4879 is also very isolated. Its nearest neighbour, Leo A, is about 2.3 million light years away, roughly the gap between the Andromeda Galaxy and the Milky Way. Because it has not interacted with other galaxies, it offers a clean laboratory for studying how stars form without outside disturbance.

Its history is puzzling. Studies show a lot of star formation in the first 4 billion years after the Big Bang, then a strange lull of nine billion years with little star birth, ending with a fresh burst that began 1 billion years ago. Why it behaved this way is still unknown.
explore: Because UGC 4879 has not interacted with any surrounding galaxies, its star formation is not complicated by outside influences, which makes it a useful laboratory for astronomers trying to understand how starbirth works across the Universe.

caption: The interacting galaxy NGC 5291 and its surroundings, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: This image from ESO's Very Large Telescope shows the aftermath of a galactic collision that happened 360 million years ago. At the centre is the elliptical galaxy NGC 5291, surrounded by debris thrown out in the crash.
Among that debris is a young dwarf galaxy, which shows up as a bright clump on the right-hand side of the picture. ESO describes it as both rare and mysterious.

Galaxies like it are expected to have been common in the early Universe. Those distant examples, however, are usually too faint and too far away for current telescopes to observe. Finding one close enough to study in detail gives astronomers a valuable chance to learn about a type of galaxy that may have been widespread long ago. NGC 5291 lies in the constellation of Centaurus, and the picture was made with the FORS2 instrument on the VLT.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 7640, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows NGC 7640, a galaxy in the constellation of Andromeda. The name can cause confusion, since the constellation is one of the 88 modern constellations and not to be mixed up with our neighbour the Andromeda Galaxy.

Astronomers sort galaxies by shape and structure, and NGC 7640 is a barred spiral. In galaxies of this type, the spiral arms fan out not from a round core but from an elongated bar that runs through the centre. Our own Milky Way is a barred spiral too.

NGC 7640 may not look much like a spiral here. That is because of the angle from which we, and Hubble, see it. Galaxies are rarely turned face-on towards us, and when they are tilted, features such as spiral arms become harder to make out.
explore: NGC 7640 lies about 30 million light-years away. The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys in visible and near-infrared light.
