understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble shows fine structure that no eye at a telescope could pick out.

alt: A tilted spiral galaxy seen at an angle, so its arms are hard to make out.

caption: The spiral galaxy ESO 486-21, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Alone in a field of stars at the centre of this image sits the galaxy ESO 486-21. It is a spiral, though its structure is somewhat irregular and poorly defined, and it lies some 30 million light-years from Earth.

Hubble observed it during the Legacy ExtraGalactic UV Survey, or LEGUS, which covered 50 nearby galaxies that are forming stars. The sample was chosen to include a wide variety of shapes, star formation rates and masses. Astronomers use such data to learn how stars form and evolve inside clusters, and how that affects their galaxies and the wider Universe.
ESO 486-21 was a natural choice because it is making new stars. Stars form when large clouds of gas and dust inside a galaxy collapse inwards, and such clouds show up in pink.
explore: LEGUS used two Hubble cameras at once. Wide Field Camera 3 studied the main target, while the Advanced Camera for Surveys, rather than sitting idle, looked at a patch of sky just beside it, collecting extra so-called parallel fields. Such parallel fields were also important for Hubble's Frontier Fields programme, which used gravitational lensing by massive galaxy clusters to study distant objects.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters from 275 to 814 nm, spanning ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light, plus a filter that isolates glowing hydrogen. The colours assigned to each filter are not published, though the caption notes the gas and dust clouds appear pink.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and this faint galaxy could not be seen in such detail without Hubble.

alt: An irregular spiral galaxy with pink patches of gas and dust at the centre of a star-filled field.

caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy IC 755, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A long, thin stream of stars, gas and dust crosses this Hubble image. It is IC 755, a spiral galaxy seen edge-on.

In 1999 a star in IC 755 exploded as a supernova, SN 1999an, found by the Beijing Astronomical Observatory Supernova Survey. Three years later, Hubble studied the region where the explosion happened. Because the galaxy is tilted edge-on, many objects in between blocked the view, making this a difficult target. Even so, the data suggest the star may have been about 20 times the mass of the Sun and around 14 million years old when it exploded.

SN 1999an was a Type II supernova, a violent event that ends the life of a massive star. Explosions like this matter for how galaxies evolve. They create many elements and fling them far across space, and their shockwaves stir up material in the galaxy and may trigger new star formation.
explore: Galaxies like IC 755 contain billions of stars, and many of them will one day become supernovae, spending their final moments seeding the Universe with new material. The field of view here is 3.3 x 1.5 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image was made with the Wide Field Camera of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Blue-filter exposures (F435W) are shown in blue, yellow-green (F555W) in green, and near-infrared (F814W) in red.
understand.eye: The red channel is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the exposures of 430 seconds per filter reveal far more than an eye could see.

alt: A thin, elongated edge-on galaxy crossing the frame, a streak of stars, gas and dust.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2758, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Bright blue stars dot the loosely wound spiral arms of the small galaxy NGC 2758 in this sharp Hubble image. To the upper left is a bright companion dwarf galaxy, and many more distant galaxies fill the background.

NGC 2758 is found in Hydra, the Sea Serpent, which is the biggest and longest of all the constellations. It was first seen in the 1880s by the American astronomer Frank Muller, working at the McCormick Observatory in Virginia.

The galaxy is near enough for its structure to be seen very clearly, which makes it a fine example of a spiral. Hubble observed it as part of a study of the redder central bulge found in galaxies, looking at how these central regions form and change over time. A galaxy's bulge is its dense inner concentration of stars, and comparing bulges across many galaxies helps astronomers piece together how whole galaxies grow.
explore: The image was made from Hubble exposures through a blue filter (F435W) and a near-infrared filter (F814W), each lasting 1050 s. The field of view is about 3.4 arcminutes across, and the galaxy lies about 120 million light-years away.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue (F435W) and near-infrared (F814W) filters, with a green channel made up from them. The exact colour mapping is not published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and long exposures through each filter gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: A small spiral galaxy with blue stars in loose arms, a bright dwarf galaxy to the upper left and faint galaxies in the background.

caption: The irregular dwarf galaxy UGC 4459, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The diffuse, disorganised cloud of stars in this Hubble image is UGC 4459, an irregular dwarf galaxy about 11 million light-years away in Ursa Major. It has no clear structure, with no central bulge of tightly packed stars and no trace of spiral arms.

Irregular dwarfs get less attention than spiral and elliptical galaxies, yet they are among the most common galaxies in the Universe. Astronomers suspect that some were once spirals or ellipticals that were later pulled out of shape by the gravity of nearby objects.

UGC 4459 holds young blue stars and older red ones, several billion in all. That sounds like a lot until you set it beside the Milky Way, home to 200 to 400 billion stars. Hubble observations show that small galaxies like this form stars at a very low rate, having turned only a little of their original gas into stars.
explore: That makes them useful for studying conditions similar to the early Universe and the process of star formation itself. Ursa Major also contains the Pinwheel Galaxy (M101), the Owl Nebula (M97), and Messier 81 and Messier 82, along with other members of the M81 group.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble data from Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys, with filters from 275 to 814 nm spanning ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and Hubble resolves individual stars in a galaxy that would look like a faint smudge otherwise.

alt: A diffuse, shapeless cloud of blue and red stars forming a dwarf galaxy.

caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy NGC 4163, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A swarm of young, blue stars fills this Hubble view of NGC 4163, a diffuse dwarf irregular galaxy. It belongs to a group of dwarf galaxies that lie near our Milky Way, and it is located roughly 10 million light-years away, in the constellation of Canes Venatici.

Dwarf irregular galaxies are small galaxies without a clear shape. They have no neat spiral arms and no smooth, rounded form like an elliptical galaxy. Instead, their stars are spread in a loose, uneven way, which is why this one looks so diffuse.

Blue stars are usually young and hot, so a crowd of them points to fairly recent star formation within the galaxy. At roughly 10 million light-years, NGC 4163 counts as a close neighbour by astronomical standards.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters at 475, 606 and 814 nm, in visible and near-infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble resolves individual stars in this galaxy that would blend into a faint haze without it.

alt: A loose swarm of blue stars forming a small, diffuse galaxy.

caption: The spiral galaxy LEDA 2046648 and a crowded galaxy field, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Stars and galaxies in many colours, mostly shades of orange, crowd this Webb image, with bright stars wearing Webb's six-pointed diffraction spikes. Along the bottom is a large, detailed spiral seen at an angle, with a galaxy about a quarter of its size just below. Both have glowing cores, and star formation lights up their arms.
The large spiral is LEDA 2046648, a little over a billion light-years away in Hercules. Around it are many smaller, more distant galaxies, from full spirals to faint smudges.

Studying distant galaxies in the early Universe is one of Webb's main goals. Their light is redshifted to infrared wavelengths, which Webb's keen infrared vision can capture, letting it look back in time. Comparing those galaxies with nearby ones will help astronomers learn how galaxies grew into the structures seen today, and Webb will also study how heavy elements built up as galaxies evolved.
explore: This picture came from the commissioning of Webb's NIRISS instrument. While NIRISS observed a well-studied white dwarf, WD1657+343, the Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam) took this image in parallel, letting astronomers compare data from the two instruments and check how NIRISS performs.

understand.summary: This image was taken in near-infrared light by Webb's NIRCam. Light at 1.5 μm is shown as blue, 2.0 μm as cyan, 2.77 μm as yellow and 3.56 μm as red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye. The colours are assigned so that shorter infrared wavelengths look bluer and longer ones redder.

alt: A dark field crowded with stars and galaxies, mostly orange, with a large spiral galaxy seen at an angle along the bottom and a smaller galaxy just beneath it.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 5806 and supernova SN 2004dg, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: NGC 5806, the spiral galaxy in this Hubble image, lies in Virgo, around 80 million light years from Earth. Near the bottom of the galaxy is a faint yellowish dot, the afterglow of SN 2004dg, a supernova produced when a giant star exploded at the end of its life in 2004.

The exposures were taken in early 2005 to help pin down the supernova's position. NGC 5806 was picked for a study of supernovae because Hubble's archive already held sharp images of it from before the star exploded. Supernovae are fairly rare and cannot be predicted with any accuracy, so before-and-after views like these are very valuable.

Otherwise the galaxy is fairly ordinary, neither especially large nor small, close nor distant. Its central bulge is a disc-type bulge, where the spiral pattern continues right into the centre instead of giving way to a large elliptical bulge of stars.
explore: NGC 5806 also has an active galactic nucleus, where a supermassive black hole draws in matter that heats up and gives off powerful radiation as it spirals inwards. Andre van der Hoeven submitted a version of this image to the Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition, which invited enthusiasts to search Hubble's archive for unseen images.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, combining exposures in visible and infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is infrared, invisible to the eye, and a supernova in a galaxy this distant is far too faint to see without a large telescope.

alt: A spiral galaxy with a faint yellowish dot near its lower edge marking a supernova.

caption: The twisting gas filaments of NGC 5972, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Twisting through the darkness like a disturbed double helix, the ionised gas around the galaxy NGC 5972 forms an unusual structure. The gas seems to reel through space as if shaken by some huge disturbance, possibly a merger with another galaxy.

These sweeping trails glow in H-alpha light and in light from doubly ionised oxygen, both usually expected where stars are born and die. They stretch far beyond the stars that make up the main body of the galaxy. They reach so far that when Hubble used the filter needed to see the gas, the full extent of the clouds did not fit within its field of view.

NGC 5972 also has an active galactic nucleus. A supermassive black hole sits at its centre, and material in the disc swirling around it moves so violently that twin beams of plasma shoot out in opposite directions at close to the speed of light.
explore: Because such jets carry enormous amounts of energy, they are best imaged at radio wavelengths, where they can form structures that dwarf their host galaxies. ESA points to Cygnus A, imaged by the NRAO Very Large Array, as an example. There, the galaxy's nucleus looks tiny beside its vast jets and lobes.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble data from the Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, using broad filters and narrow filters that isolate glowing hydrogen and oxygen gas. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The narrow filters isolate the specific glow of hydrogen and oxygen gas, making faint filaments stand out that would be far too dim for the eye.

alt: A galaxy surrounded by twisting filaments of glowing gas that extend far beyond its stars, some reaching the edge of the frame.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 3583, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two spiral arms twist outwards from the barred spiral galaxy NGC 3583 in this Hubble image. The galaxy lies 98 million light-years from the Milky Way, in the constellation of Ursa Major.

Two supernovae have exploded in NGC 3583, one in 1975 and a second, more recent one in 2015, though neither is visible. Supernovae can arise in a few different ways. Both of these came from binary star systems, pairs of stars in orbit around each other.

In each case, one member of the pair was a white dwarf, the leftover core of a Sun-like star. The white dwarf pulled material from its companion star and kept gaining mass until it reached a maximum limit. At that point it collapsed inwards and then blew apart in a brilliant supernova. The two explosions came from two separate binary systems within the same galaxy.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters at 350, 555 and 814 nm, from near-ultraviolet to near-infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Some of this light lies outside the range the eye can see, and Hubble shows structure in this distant galaxy that no eye could make out.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with two arms twisting out from a central bar.

caption: The Eagle, Omega and Sharpless 2-54 nebulae, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Three glowing clouds of gas share this image from ESO's VLT Survey Telescope. On the right is the faint nebula Sharpless 2-54. In the centre sits the famous Eagle Nebula, Messier 16, and to the left is the Omega Nebula, Messier 17.
The image is enormous, containing three gigapixels, and takes in a wide stretch of sky at once.

The two Messier objects are well known, while Sharpless 2-54 is much less familiar. Together, the three make up only part of a vast complex of gas and dust. Inside it, new stars are forming, and their light makes the surrounding gas glow. Nebulae like these are stellar nurseries. Dense clouds collapse under gravity to form stars, and the hottest young stars then light up and sculpt the gas that remains into glowing shapes like these.
explore: The VLT Survey Telescope is designed to photograph large areas of sky in detail, which makes it well suited to showing how separate, well-known nebulae belong to a single connected region of star formation.

understand.summary: This image comes from the OmegaCAM camera on ESO's VLT Survey Telescope, using visible-light filters including one that isolates glowing hydrogen. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: These nebulae are faint to the eye, and the camera's long exposures and hydrogen filter bring out glowing gas that would otherwise be hard to see.

alt: A wide view of three glowing nebulae of gas and dust side by side across a starry field.

caption: The Eagle Nebula in infrared, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: At the centre of this infrared view of the Eagle Nebula, also called Messier 16, stand the famous Pillars of Creation, joined by several other pillars in the same star-forming region. Stars crowd the whole frame. At upper right, a cluster of bright blue stars marks NGC 6611, whose massive, hot stars light up the pillars.

The colours tell the stars apart. Blue ones belong either to the young cluster NGC 6611 or are foreground stars along our line of sight. Most stars look fainter and yellower. They are ordinary stars far behind M16, seen through the clouds from which the cluster formed. A few very red stars are either very young and still wrapped in gas and dust, or brighter background stars shining through it.
The picture is a mosaic of 144 images from the ISAAC instrument on the VLT's Antu telescope, sensitive enough to detect young stars of all masses.
explore: The Eagle Nebula lies in the constellation of Serpens, about 6,500 light-years away. The mosaic covers roughly 17 x 17 light-years, and the image sharpness reaches about 0.35 arcseconds. To bring out faint gas, the brightness of each band was compressed before the colours were combined.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image comes from the ISAAC instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. The Js band (1.24 μm) is shown as blue, H (1.65 μm) as green and Ks (2.16 μm) as red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it passes through dust more easily than visible light, revealing stars inside and behind the clouds.

alt: An infrared view of a nebula with pillars at the centre, a cluster of blue stars at upper right and a dense field of yellow and red stars.
flags: distance mismatch: metadata 7000 vs caption about 6,500 light-years

caption: The star cluster R136 in the 30 Doradus Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hundreds of brilliant blue stars sit among warm, glowing clouds in this Hubble view, the most detailed yet of the largest stellar nursery in our galactic neighbourhood. The young cluster at its heart, R136, has existed for only a few million years and lies in the 30 Doradus Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
Many of these blue stars are among the most massive known, several over 100 times the mass of the Sun. They will probably explode as supernovae within a few million years.

Their ultraviolet light and fierce stellar winds are carving deep cavities in the hydrogen cloud where they were born. The result is a landscape of pillars, ridges and valleys, with a dark central area shaped roughly like a holiday tree. When the winds slam into dense walls of gas they produce shocks, which may be setting off a new wave of star birth.
explore: The Large Magellanic Cloud's motion around the Milky Way may have triggered the cluster's birth, by compressing its gas through gravity or by pressure as it ploughed through our galaxy's halo. R136 is a rare nearby example of the super star clusters common in the early Universe. The image spans about 100 light-years.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in ultraviolet, visible and red light. Blue shows light from the hottest, most massive stars, green the glow of oxygen, and red fluorescing hydrogen.
understand.eye: Part of this light is ultraviolet, invisible to the eye, and the colours were chosen to separate different gases rather than to show what the eye would see.

alt: A cluster of bright blue stars amid glowing clouds carved into pillars, ridges and valleys, with a dark tree-shaped region near the centre.

caption: The Crab Nebula, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: Tangled filaments fill this wide view of the Crab Nebula, also known as Messier 1, NGC 1952 and Taurus A. These threads are the debris of a star that exploded as a supernova, seen by Chinese astronomers in 1054, and they are still flying outwards at about 1500 kilometres per second.

Hidden at the heart of the nebula, behind foreground filaments of helium and hydrogen, are two faint stars. One of them, the Crab Pulsar, is what powers the nebula today. It is the small, dense remains of the star that exploded, now only about 20 kilometres wide and spinning 30 times every second.

The pulsar sends out pulses of radiation across all wavelengths, from radio waves up to gamma rays, where it ranks among the brightest sources in the sky. Its radiation is strong enough to push a wave of material that is reshaping the inner nebula.
explore: Those inner structures change so quickly that astronomers can watch them alter shape, a rare chance, since most astronomical changes take far too long to observe. The Wide Field Imager data used here were picked from the ESO archive by Manu Mejias for the Hidden Treasures competition.

understand.summary: This image uses data from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla, taken in visible light through several filters, including one for glowing hydrogen. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The Crab Nebula is too faint to see with the naked eye, and the filaments only show this clearly in long telescope exposures.

alt: A nebula of tangled, glowing filaments against a field of stars.

caption: The N 70 superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: This three-colour image shows N 70, a glowing superbubble of interstellar gas in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way in the southern sky. The bubble is about 300 light-years across.

N 70 was blown out by winds from hot, massive stars and by supernova explosions, and its interior is filled with thin, hot gas that is still expanding. Objects like this give astronomers an excellent chance to study how the life cycles of stars are linked to the way whole galaxies evolve.

Very massive stars have a big effect on their surroundings. Their winds and explosions stir and mix the clouds of gas and dust between the stars. In doing so they leave a lasting mark on where future generations of stars and planetary systems will form, and on what those new stars will be made of.
explore: The image was built from CCD frames taken with the FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. ESO's caption puts the Large Magellanic Cloud at about 160,000 light-years from us.

understand.summary: This image comes from the FORS2 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, using B, V and hydrogen-alpha filters in visible light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen filter isolates the glow of the gas, and the telescope's exposures reveal a bubble far too faint to see by eye.

alt: A glowing bubble of gas among stars.

caption: The star-forming region NGC 346, imaged by XMM-Newton, the New Technology Telescope and Spitzer
story: Different kinds of light swirl together like watercolours in this portrait of NGC 346, a bright star-forming region. The image combines data from three telescopes, and it has revealed new information about how stars form.

Found in the Small Magellanic Cloud, NGC 346 is 210,000 light-years from us. That galaxy is a dwarf galaxy neighbouring the Milky Way. X-rays from ESA's XMM-Newton appear in blue, visible light from ESO's New Technology Telescope in green, and infrared light from NASA's Spitzer in red.

Each colour traces something different. The infrared shows cold dust, the visible light marks glowing gas, and the X-rays reveal very hot gas. Ordinary stars look like blue dots with white middles, while young stars still cocooned in dust look like red dots with white middles. Putting the three views together lets astronomers see the cold, warm and hot parts of a star-forming region at once.
explore: No single telescope could produce this view on its own. X-rays and much of the infrared are blocked by Earth's atmosphere, so two of the three datasets had to come from space observatories.

understand.summary: This composite combines X-rays from ESA's XMM-Newton (blue), visible light from ESO's New Technology Telescope (green) and infrared from NASA's Spitzer (red).
understand.eye: The eye sees only the visible part. X-rays and infrared are invisible, so most of what this image shows could never be seen directly.

caption: The Tarantula Nebula, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: This view from ESO's VLT Survey Telescope shows the Tarantula Nebula, a gigantic star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy of the Milky Way. It lies in the direction of the constellation Dorado.

An astonishing number of massive stars are born in the Tarantula. Some of them might reach masses of up to 300 times that of the Sun, although that figure is a possibility rather than a firm measurement.

Star-forming regions like this are vast clouds of gas and dust. Dense pockets collapse under their own gravity to form new stars, and the most massive of these newborn stars pour out energy that makes the surrounding gas glow. In the Tarantula, that process has produced an unusually large crop of heavyweight stars.

understand.summary: This image comes from the OmegaCAM camera on ESO's VLT Survey Telescope, using visible and near-infrared filters plus one that isolates glowing hydrogen. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: A survey telescope's exposures gather far more light than the eye, and the hydrogen filter brings out glowing gas in detail no eye could see.

alt: A large, glowing star-forming nebula in a neighbouring galaxy.

caption: The star cluster RCW 38 in infrared light, imaged by the VISTA telescope
story: Gas, dust and stars mix into a rich, tangled landscape in this 80-million-pixel picture of the star cluster RCW 38, in the constellation Vela. The cluster is young, holds about 2000 stars and is full of star-forming activity.

The image was taken with ESO's Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy (VISTA) in Chile's Atacama Desert. VISTA observes in infrared light, which can pass through most of the dust in this region. In visible light, that dust would block much of the view.

Looking behind the dust, VISTA reveals young stars still wrapped in dusty cocoons. It also shows cold objects called brown dwarfs, sometimes described as failed stars because they never became massive enough to shine like true stars. Together they show what goes on inside a young stellar nursery.
scaleExtra: RCW 38 is about 5500 light-years away, according to ESO.

understand.summary: This image comes from the VIRCAM camera on ESO's VISTA telescope, in near-infrared light through J (1.25 μm), H (1.65 μm) and Ks (2.15 μm) filters. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, but it lets VISTA see through dust that would hide these stars in visible light.

alt: A dense star field with glowing gas and dark dust around a young star cluster.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6752, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Countless stars crowd this Hubble image of NGC 6752, a globular cluster, a dense ball of stars bound by gravity. At over 10 billion years old, it is one of the most ancient star clusters known, and has been shining for well over twice as long as our Solar System has existed.

The cluster is rich in blue stragglers, and some are visible here. These stars look younger than their neighbours, even though models suggest most stars in a globular cluster formed at about the same time. Where they come from is something of a mystery.

NGC 6752 may help explain them. A very high share of the stars in its core, up to 38%, appear to be binary systems, pairs of stars orbiting each other. In such a crowded, turbulent region, collisions between stars could produce the many blue stragglers seen there.
explore: NGC 6752 lies 13 000 light-years away in the constellation of Pavo, but Hubble's sharp images let astronomers study it and its puzzling blue stragglers in detail.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters at 555, 606 and 814 nm, in visible and near-infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble separates individual stars that would blur together through a small telescope.

alt: A dense field of countless stars forming a globular cluster.

caption: The ring around supernova 1987A, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows a ring of gas around supernova 1987A. The star's explosion was seen on February 23, 1987. Its home is an irregular galaxy that orbits the Milky Way, the Large Magellanic Cloud.

The picture was taken with the European Space Agency's Faint Object Camera. With a resolution of 0.07 arcseconds, Hubble could see that the ring is clumpy, which tells astronomers that the material in it is not spread out evenly.

A supernova is the explosion of a star, and the gas around it can hold clues about the star's life before it blew up. Those clumps are one such clue about the star's past, and only the sharpness of Hubble's view could reveal them in this nearby galaxy.

understand.summary: This image was taken with the Faint Object Camera on the Hubble Space Telescope. The filters and colour mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The ring is far too small and faint to be seen by eye. Only a space telescope's sharp resolution reveals its clumpy structure.

alt: A small ring of gas around the site of a supernova.

caption: The galaxies NGC 5011B and NGC 5011C, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two galaxies appear side by side against a starry background in this Hubble image, with the spiral NGC 5011B on the right and the bluish NGC 5011C at the centre. They look like neighbours, but that is an illusion.

NGC 5011B belongs to the Centaurus Cluster of galaxies, 156 million light-years away. For years NGC 5011C was assumed to be part of that cluster too, but it was puzzling. It was as faint as a nearby dwarf galaxy but as large as an early-type spiral. And if the pair really were close together, astronomers would expect signs of interaction between them. There were none.

The answer came from measuring how fast each galaxy is moving away from us. NGC 5011C is receding much more slowly, in step with the nearby Centaurus A group, 13 million light-years away. It is a nearby dwarf galaxy, not a distant cluster member.
explore: The stars in NGC 5011C add up to only about ten million solar masses. The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through visible and infrared filters.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters at 606 and 814 nm, in visible and near-infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and like the eye, a single image cannot show depth, which is why these galaxies seem to be neighbours.

alt: A spiral galaxy on the right and a bluish, diffuse galaxy at the centre against a starry background.

caption: The low surface brightness galaxy UGC 477, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows UGC 477, a galaxy in Pisces lying just over 110 million light-years from Earth. It is a low surface brightness galaxy, a type whose light is spread thinly, making it far more diffuse than galaxies such as Andromeda or the Milky Way.

Their surface brightness can be as much as 250 times fainter than the night sky itself, so they are very hard to detect. Mike Disney proposed they existed in 1976, but they were only confirmed in 1986, with the discovery of the galaxy Malin 1.

Most of their matter is hydrogen gas, not stars, and their centres lack the crowd of stars found in the bulges of normal spirals. Astronomers suspect this is because they tend to sit in empty regions, where fewer encounters and mergers have triggered intense star formation. They appear to be dominated by dark matter.
explore: That makes galaxies like UGC 477 useful for studying dark matter, the invisible substance thought to make up much of the mass in galaxies. Because they are so faint, they have long been underrepresented in galaxy surveys, and their importance has been recognised only fairly recently.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters at 475 and 775 nm, in visible and near-infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: A galaxy fainter than the night sky's own glow is effectively invisible to the eye. Only long, sensitive exposures reveal it.

alt: A faint, diffuse galaxy seen by Hubble.

caption: An elliptical galaxy in the Capodimonte Deep Field, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This close-up shows an elliptical galaxy on the western, right-hand side of a larger survey image called the Capodimonte Deep Field. Many tiny objects surround the galaxy, and these may be globular clusters, dense balls of old stars that orbit galaxies. A fuzzy object on the right edge of the frame may be a dwarf spheroidal galaxy, a small, faint and roughly round kind of galaxy.
Elliptical galaxies are smooth, rounded collections of stars without spiral arms. This one is not alone, and is surrounded by a crowd of much smaller objects.

The picture is a section of a much wider image, shown at the camera's original scale. Its purpose is partly to show how much information a single wide-field image holds, since even a small cut-out reveals a galaxy with its own retinue of smaller objects.
explore: The field shown measures about 6 by 5 arcminutes on the sky. The identifications are tentative. The tiny objects and the fuzzy one at the edge are possible globular clusters and a possible dwarf galaxy, not confirmed ones.

alt: An elliptical galaxy surrounded by many tiny points of light, with a fuzzy object at the right edge.
